title: 1 year building a browser AI RPG — why the LLM doesn't own the state
author: SnooDoubts748
selftext:
After about a year of building Loreon — a browser interactive-fiction RPG — the part I keep coming back to is the split between what the LLM does and what it doesn't.

The model writes the prose between scenes. It does NOT own state. Inventory, location, objectives, and time are structured data held by a separate engine, read and written explicitly each turn. State is rendered as visible chips in the UI, and the next prompt to the model is built from that state, not from raw chat history.

Reason for the split: pure-chat AI games drift after \~10–20 turns — items reappear, locations blur, objectives quietly die. Putting state in a structured layer keeps the world canonical regardless of what the model "remembers."

Stack: Bun monorepo, Svelte player app, custom CMS for scenarios, Paddle billing, browser-only. Guest mode for the first scenes: [https://loreon.online](https://loreon.online)

Curious — has anyone here solved state-drift with a different architecture? I've seen people try summary-stuffing into context, but it degrades smoothly until it doesn't.

comments.author: Cubey42

replies.author: TurnYourBrightsOFF
replies.body: Very unfortunate use of time.  Nowadays, with all the learning material available, a beginner can realistically learn enough coding to manually make decent interactive fiction games in way under a year (and that's without a pre-made engine). Then you'd also have practical development skills beyond just prompting AI.  At very least, the OP should have spent a large portion of that time researching UX/UI, marketing and on how to use properly use AI as a development tool.

comments.author: Top_Issue_7032
comments.body: Why did you put a mobile view inside of a browser? Why not just learn and use responsive design?

replies.author: SnooDoubts748
replies.body: It's a deliberate mobile-first product, the page itself says "MOBILE FIRST / Best experience on your phone" and offers a QR code to continue there. A native wider desktop layout is on the roadmap, but with limited time I prioritized making the mobile experience excellent over making the desktop view a parallel design. Fair criticism that the choice isn't obvious if you don't read the panel.

replies.author: Top_Issue_7032
replies.body: Mobile-first \*is\* responsive design. Design for the smallest viewport, scale up. A fixed phone-width layout in a desktop browser is a well-known anti-pattern, not a methodology.

comments.author: notsofst
comments.body:
No, the AI can't manage state. It's basically an approximation machine, so anything that needs to be exact is going to fail. Traditional software is great at things that need to be exact.

So it makes sense to pair the two together and have them use tool calling and structured json so each one can do what it's best at.

I'm working on something similar, I'll send you a link when the site's up.

replies.author: SnooDoubts748
replies.body: Yeah, same conclusion: anything that needs to be canonical (inventory, location, time) can't live in the model's working memory, it has to be tool-call-able state the model reads from. What approach are you taking - strict JSON schema for state ops, or freeform tool calls with validation? Would love the link when your site is up.

replies.author: notsofst
replies.body: I have llms with tools and llms that throw events to a stateful backend. I find myself using the event system for almost everything now, though. The LLM gets a state snapshot, has a job/prompt, returns json, and then I parse the results and trigger events and state changes off it.

replies.author: leather-armor
replies.body: Paste it here when it's done! I'll be glad to help, even if just being a BETA user

comments.author: MeasIIDX
comments.body:
Interesting concept and it makes me think about how you handle reader-input.

I asked it a few technical questions when it gave me an opportunity to do so but the story continued on without referring to what I wrote. Does the player's free-input truly affect the story or is it smoke and mirrors and the story is just on rails?

It's neat but not for me. Best of luck!

replies.author: SnooDoubts748
replies.body: Could you share roughly what you typed? The narrator stays scoped inside the scenario by design, meta or out-of-character queries to the system don't break the fourth wall, that's intentional. But in-character input (asking an NPC something, taking an action, making a choice) should flow into the next scene's state. If yours was in-character and got ignored, that's a real bug. If it was meta-probing, the silence was the intended boundary. Hard to tell from the comment alone.

replies.author: MeasIIDX
replies.body:
It was actually probing to see how well the responses were harnessed and honestly you've done a great job focusing on what is and isn't viable.

I asked about dispatching a background job during migration for back-end systems while interacting with a dragon on the fantasy story.

It's the same question I ask every AI input I see because I'm curious on how the harnesses treat it.

The character did end up saying "Dispatched? What are you mumbling about." And continued on with the story. That's what made me think how on-rails the story is since it decided to continue with my absurd input.

I promise I wasn't trying to be malicious but it was more harness-curiosity than anything else. I can see the appeal for those who want this kind of immersion.

comments.author: leather-armor
comments.body:
I'm doing something similar myself, but I keep going back and forth on what AI should own vs deterministic code. In the end, if you can't offer much freedom, the user is better off playing BG3. In my mind, the tradeoff is that you can do anything, freeroam, ignore a quest, call the guards, and so on, so although hard numbers and statuses certainly need to be deterministic and code-reliant, it's not clear to me exactly where I'm splitting the line.

My thing is [https://leatherarmor.io/r](https://leatherarmor.io/r)   
  
I'm trying to make it more rule-heavy and still experimenting on how much I care if the user goes "Oh, I try to mount the dragon" when there is no dragon there. I mean, should I stop the player from breaking the world? Because if he wants to and thinks it will be fun... anyway, I don't know.

As for state-drift, I'm playing around with creative vector similarity to store and update certain "world-state facts", but I'm still experimenting.
